elements.char: We make a few key assumptions inspired by dsDNA-dsDNA pairing
elements.label: text

elements.char: in vivo
elements.label: text

elements.char: . First, we note
elements.label: text

elements.char: that the crowded environment of the cell ensures that different regions of the genome collide
elements.label: text

elements.char: frequently. We model each collision as an opportunity for homology testing. We assume that
elements.label: text

elements.char: binding of homologous dsDNA regions promotes some function that is performed by a molec-
elements.label: text

elements.char: ular machinery, provided that pairing of the two dsDNA regions is sufficiently persistent. We
elements.label: text

elements.char: ask how long it takes for two homologous regions in a bacterial chromosome to find each
elements.label: text

elements.char: other and stay bound long enough for that machinery to act. We model this action as an irre-
elements.label: text

elements.char: versible transition that makes the pairing permanent. RecA mediated homologous repair in
elements.label: text

elements.char: bacteria may be an example of such a process. [20].
elements.label: text

elements.char: Theoretical work that describes homology dependent pairing of dsDNA highlight the
elements.label: text

elements.char: importance of the helical nature of these molecules [9, 10, 21, 22]. The helical structure limits
elements.label: text

elements.char: the interaction sites to roughly a few bases per helical turn, creating an interacting system in
elements.label: text

elements.char: which discrete periodically spaced binding sites are separated by non-interacting zones. We
elements.label: text

elements.char: therefore model a collision between two regions of bacterial chromosomes as a local interac-
elements.label: text

elements.char: tion between two rigid ‘rods’ carrying a linear array of equally spaced binding sites. The bind-
elements.label: text

elements.char: ing sites on the rods are separated by 3.4 nm, on the assumption that two dsDNA molecules
elements.label: text

elements.char: interact roughly once per helical turn. The total length of the rods is 17 binding sites or 57.8
elements.label: text

elements.char: nm, which is comparable to measured values for the persistence length of dsDNA. The energy
elements.label: text

elements.char: associated with interaction between the two rods is given by the sum of interactions among
elements.label: text

elements.char: their binding sites, which is taken to be exponentially decaying with distance. Thus, in this
elements.label: text

elements.char: model the interaction energy between the two molecules depends only on two degrees of free-
elements.label: text

elements.char: dom: the planar angle between the two rods, and the distance between their centers. Together,
elements.label: text

elements.char: these assumptions simplify the analysis of this model considerably, providing clear results that
elements.label: text

elements.char: are easy to interpret.
